text: Here before you lies the Black Mausoleum, the final resting place of Sir George Mackenzie, or better known today as Bloody Mackenzie. Born in Dundee in 1636, Mackenzie grew to be a well-respected lawyer and politician. He gained notoriety for his involvement in the Scottish witch trials, particularly his defence of the alleged witch maevia. His prominence grew due to his published essays and legal writings, and is even credited with writing the first Scottish novel, Artina. He was also acknowledged for assisting in the establishment of the Advocates' Library, now part of the National Library of Scotland. He served as a member of the Scottish Parliament, received the knighthood, and eventually rose to the role of Lord Advocate. However, all these accomplishments have faded in time. History remembers him for his ruthlessness. His role as Lord Advocate made Mackenzie responsible for leading the crown's relentless prosecution of those who refused to renounce the National Covenant. He oversaw the trials of countless Covenanters, most of whom faced mass imprisonment, transportation overseas, torture, or execution for their beliefs. Almost 500 of the Covenanters imprisoned here in the Covenanters' prison, within Greyfriars, were sent there by the direct order of Mackenzie himself. But thousands overall suffered under his harsh rulings. His brutal and bloodthirsty pursuit of all religious dissonance earned him the infamous nickname, Bloody Mackenzie. The title became his lasting legacy, casting a long shadow over all else he achieved in life. After his death, the black mausoleum became his final resting place. Seen as one of the finest examples of 17th century cemetery architecture, it is an ominous monument to someone remembered as a black-hearted man. The mausoleum is positioned right next to what was the boundary wall of the prison itself. George Mackenzie requested this site for burial, reasoning that he was very proud of what he accomplished in his persecution of the Covenanters. He remained here undisturbed for three centuries. Until, in 1999, on a cold, stormy night, a homeless man wandered through Greyfriars' kirkyard in the hopes of finding somewhere warm to shelter for the night. Spotting the black mausoleum and deciding that might be the perfect place to rest his head, he first tried to open the doors. Finding them locked, he ventured around the back of the tombs by climbing through a small hole that descended the stairs to the tomb below, holding the very coffin of Mackenzie himself. As he approached the coffin, the floor gave way and he plummeted down into the darkness into a chamber below. Feeling something bumpy underneath his feet, the man was horrified to find he was atop a large pile of bodies. He saw that some of the corpses were still somewhat fleshy, believed to be due to the lack of oxygen flow to the chamber, slowing down the decomposition process. It has been theorised he had fallen into a mass grave for bubonic plague victims. The next morning, two people who were opening the church noticed the sound of a... coming from the mausoleum. When they opened the doors to investigate, they saw the homeless man, pale-faced, sitting stiffly upright. He was covered in bloody scratches and trembling all over. His foot shaking caused the tapping sound against the door. All he could repeat, over and over again, in a shaking voice, was... That face! The man awoke the very ghost of George Mackenzie that night, and strange events have never ceased since. His poltergeist causes havoc to those who dare approach his tomb. Since 1999, there are reports of over 350 documented attacks, with visitors experiencing feeling their hair pulled or their limbs being scratched, or the feeling of being pushed or shelved by unseen forces, and at least 140 people have collapsed. Many leave to find inexplicable bruises or scratches upon their bodies. Some just notice sudden drops in temperature, as though the spirit has passed through them. White figures have been reported being spotted, moving near the tomb and around the graves nearby, and eerie reports of knocking noises from beneath. There have also been dead animals repeatedly found near the mausoleum, showing no obvious cause of death. Even the houses surrounding the kirkyard have reported inexplicable phenomena, such as strange fires breaking out. A paranormal investigator writing a book about the Mackenzie haunting lost his notes about the poltergeist in a house fire, as though the benevolent spirit of Bloody Mackenzie himself was trying to cease his work. In the year of 2000, a spiritualist medium attempted to urge the ghosts of the kirkyard to rest, but died suddenly of a heart attack a few weeks later. Many attribute this to the legend of the Mackenzie poltergeist. There is an old Heriot School rhyme that some visitors dare recite, maybe to provoke an appearance of his spirit. If you're daring enough, go up to the bar and repeat these words. See what happens. Today, the black mausoleum has gained the reputation as one of the most haunted sites in all of the United Kingdom. Out of all the thousands of souls to be laid to rest here within the walls of Greyfriars, it is fitting that Bloody Mackenzie be the one cursed to never find peace. That concludes this chapter of the tour. We hope you have enjoyed your visit to Greyfriars Kirkyard. The gates may close behind you, but the stories you have heard tonight have lingered here for centuries. And perhaps, they'll linger with you a little while longer.
